questions.primaryUnit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt:
A language-learning app company wants to study weekly practice time among its 60,000 active adult users. The company takes a simple random sample of 800 users and records whether each user had voluntarily enabled a daily reminder before the study began. It then records each user's total practice time during the following week.

Reminder status       n   Mean weekly practice time   Standard deviation
Enabled              480          154 minutes              62 minutes
Not enabled          320          101 minutes              55 minutes

(a) Identify the population and sample. Also identify the explanatory and response variables.

(b) State a statistical question that the study can address. Calculate and interpret the observed difference in sample mean weekly practice time.

(c) Identify the study as observational or experimental. Explain why the difference in means does not establish that enabling reminders causes an increase in practice time.

(d) Describe one plausible confounding variable and explain how it could account for at least part of the observed association.

(e) Explain what the simple random sample permits the company to generalize and what the study design does not permit the company to conclude.
questions.scoringGuide:
Total Points: 10
(a) 2 points
· Point 1: Identifies the population as all 60,000 active adult users and the sample as the 800 users selected by the SRS.
· Point 2: Identifies reminder status as the categorical explanatory variable and total weekly practice time in minutes as the quantitative response variable.
(b) 2 points
· Point 1: States an appropriate statistical question about whether weekly practice time differs or is associated with voluntarily enabled reminder status among active adult users.
· Point 2: Calculates 154 − 101 = 53 minutes and interprets it: sampled users who had enabled reminders practiced an average of 53 minutes more during the week than sampled users who had not enabled reminders.
(c) 2 points
· Point 1: Identifies the study as observational because users chose their own reminder status and no treatment was randomly assigned.
· Point 2: Explains that the groups may differ in ways other than reminder status, so the observed association cannot isolate a causal effect of the reminders.
(d) 2 points
· Point 1: Identifies a plausible confounder, such as prior motivation, available free time, language-learning goals, or previous practice habits.
· Point 2: Explains how the selected confounder could be associated both with choosing to enable reminders and with spending more time practicing, offering an alternative explanation for the 53-minute difference.
(e) 2 points
· Point 1: Explains that the SRS supports generalizing the observed association to the company's 60,000 active adult users, assuming complete measurement and response.
· Point 2: States that the observational design does not support a cause-and-effect conclusion and that the result should not automatically be generalized to inactive users, children, or users of other apps.
questions.modelResponse:
The sample was randomly drawn from the company's active adult-user population, but reminder status was not assigned. The question is therefore about an association between a categorical explanatory variable and a quantitative response. The sample difference is 53 minutes, with the reminder-enabled group having the larger mean.

Random sampling and random assignment serve different purposes. The SRS supports extending the observed association to active adult users of this app. It does not make the two reminder groups comparable with respect to motivation or other preexisting characteristics. For example, highly motivated users may be more likely both to activate reminders and to practice longer, creating confounding. The data do not justify saying that reminders caused the difference.

questions.primaryUnit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt:
Wildlife biologists evaluate an acoustic classifier that flags audio segments as containing a possible canyon bat call. Human experts independently determine whether a canyon bat call is actually present. Results for 9,500 archived audio segments are shown.

Classifier flagged   Classifier did not flag   Total
Canyon bat call present              168                    42                 210
Canyon bat call absent               392                 8,898               9,290
Total                                560                 8,940               9,500

Suppose one of the 9,500 segments is selected at random.

(a) Calculate the probability that the classifier flagged the segment and the probability that a canyon bat call is actually present.

(b) Calculate the probability that the segment was flagged or actually contains a canyon bat call. Interpret the result.

(c) Given that the classifier flagged the segment, calculate the probability that a canyon bat call is actually present. Interpret the result.

(d) Given that a canyon bat call is actually present, calculate the probability that the classifier flagged the segment. Explain why this result differs from the result in part (c).

(e) Determine whether the events “classifier flagged the segment” and “canyon bat call is present” are independent. Justify your answer with probabilities from the table, and evaluate the claim, “A flagged segment has an 80% chance of containing a canyon bat call.”
questions.scoringGuide:
Total Points: 10
(a) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates P(flagged) = 560/9,500 ≈ 0.0589.
· Point 2: Calculates P(call present) = 210/9,500 ≈ 0.0221.
(b) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates P(flagged or call present) = (560 + 210 − 168)/9,500 = 602/9,500 ≈ 0.0634.
· Point 2: Interprets the result: about 6.34% of the archived segments were flagged, actually contained a canyon bat call, or both.
(c) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates P(call present | flagged) = 168/560 = 0.300.
· Point 2: Interprets the result: among flagged segments, 30.0% actually contain a canyon bat call.
(d) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates P(flagged | call present) = 168/210 = 0.800.
· Point 2: Explains that the conditioning groups differ: part (c) uses the 560 flagged segments as the denominator, whereas part (d) uses the 210 segments that actually contain a call.
(e) 2 points
· Point 1: Concludes that the events are not independent because P(call present | flagged) = 0.300 differs from P(call present) ≈ 0.0221; an equivalent valid probability comparison earns the point.
· Point 2: Rejects the claim because 80% is the probability of a flag given a true call, not the probability of a true call given a flag; the latter is only 30%.
questions.modelResponse:
The table distinguishes two conditional probabilities that are often confused. The classifier flags 560 of 9,500 segments, while only 210 of 9,500 actually contain the call. For the union in part (b), subtract the 168 segments counted in both events once. The conditional probability given a flag is 168/560 = 0.300. Reversing the condition gives 168/210 = 0.800, which measures how often the system detects a true call.

The flag and true-call events are associated because a flagged segment is much more likely to contain a call than a randomly selected segment: 0.300 versus about 0.0221. Still, the rarity of actual calls means most flags are false positives. Therefore, an 80% detection rate does not imply that 80% of flags are genuine calls.

questions.primaryUnit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.secondaryUnit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt:
A statewide association maintains a list of 2,800 independently owned bookstores. It takes a simple random sample of 240 stores and finds that 146 offer same-day pickup for online orders.

Construct and interpret a 95% confidence interval for the true proportion of all independently owned bookstores on the association's statewide list that offer same-day pickup. Use z* = 1.96.

(a) Define the population parameter and identify the appropriate confidence-interval procedure.

(b) Check the conditions for the confidence-interval procedure.

(c) Calculate the sample proportion, standard error, and margin of error, and construct the confidence interval.

(d) Interpret the 95% confidence interval in context.

(e) Use the interval to evaluate the claim that a majority of the bookstores on the statewide list offer same-day pickup.
questions.scoringGuide:
Total Points: 10
(a) 2 points
· Point 1: Defines p as the true proportion of all 2,800 independently owned bookstores on the statewide list that offer same-day pickup.
· Point 2: Selects a one-sample z confidence interval for a population proportion.
(b) 3 points
· Point 1: Cites the simple random sample.
· Point 2: Verifies the 10% condition because 240 ≤ 0.10(2,800).
· Point 3: Verifies the large-counts condition using 146 successes and 240 − 146 = 94 failures, both at least 10.
(c) 3 points
· Point 1: Calculates p̂ = 146/240 ≈ 0.6083 and SE = √[0.6083(1 − 0.6083)/240] ≈ 0.03151.
· Point 2: Calculates the margin of error as 1.96(0.03151) ≈ 0.06176.
· Point 3: Constructs 0.6083 ± 0.0618, giving the interval (0.5466, 0.6701), allowing for minor rounding differences.
(d) 1 point
· Point 1: States that the association is 95% confident that between about 54.7% and 67.0% of all independently owned bookstores on its statewide list offer same-day pickup.
(e) 1 point
· Point 1: Supports the majority claim because every plausible value in the 95% confidence interval is greater than 0.50.
questions.modelResponse:
The parameter is the statewide-list proportion, not the sample proportion. A one-proportion z interval is appropriate because the stores were randomly sampled, 240 is less than 10% of 2,800, and the sample includes well over 10 stores in each outcome category.

The estimate is 146/240 ≈ 0.6083. Its estimated standard error is approximately 0.03151, so the 95% margin of error is about 0.06176. The resulting interval is approximately (0.5466, 0.6701). This interval estimates the proportion only for bookstores on the association's list. Since the entire interval lies above 0.50, it provides evidence that a majority of the listed bookstores offer same-day pickup.

questions.secondaryUnit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt:
A school district examines the association between x, average weekly minutes of school-provided tutoring per student, and y, the percentage of students passing a common end-of-year mathematics assessment. Data for five middle schools and five high schools are shown.

School   Level    Tutoring minutes, x   Pass rate, y
M1       Middle           20                  84%
M2       Middle           25                  85%
M3       Middle           30                  86%
M4       Middle           35                  88%
M5       Middle           40                  89%
H1       High             60                  70%
H2       High             65                  71%
H3       High             70                  73%
H4       High             75                  74%
H5       High             80                  76%

Regression output:
All 10 schools:     ŷ = 93.156 − 0.271x, r = −0.811
Middle schools:     ŷ = 78.600 + 0.260x, r = 0.991
High schools:       ŷ = 51.800 + 0.300x, r = 0.993

(a) On paper, sketch a scatterplot of pass rate against tutoring minutes, using different symbols for middle and high schools. Label both axes. Describe the association for all schools together and within each school level.

(b) Interpret the slope of the regression line for all 10 schools. Use that line to predict the pass rate for a school averaging 50 tutoring minutes per student per week, and explain one reason to treat this prediction cautiously.

(c) Explain how the association can be negative for all schools combined but positive within both school levels. Identify the role of school level in this pattern.

(d) A district administrator claims, “These data show that providing more tutoring lowers mathematics pass rates.” Evaluate the claim using the study design and the regression evidence.

(e) For a high school averaging 70 tutoring minutes, calculate the predicted pass rate from both the all-school line and the high-school line. Decide which prediction is more appropriate and justify your choice.
questions.scoringGuide:
Total Points: 10
(a) 2 points
· Point 1: Sketches all 10 points with tutoring minutes on the horizontal axis and pass rate on the vertical axis, uses distinguishable symbols for the two school levels, and includes appropriate labels and scales.
· Point 2: Describes a moderately strong negative linear association when all schools are combined but very strong positive linear associations within both the middle-school and high-school groups.
(b) 2 points
· Point 1: Interprets the combined slope: across these 10 schools, each additional average tutoring minute per student is associated with a predicted decrease of about 0.271 percentage point in pass rate, on average.
· Point 2: Calculates ŷ = 93.156 − 0.271(50) = 79.606%, and notes that 50 minutes lies in a gap between the observed middle- and high-school x-values, where the combined line ignores school level.
(c) 2 points
· Point 1: Explains that high schools have both more tutoring minutes and lower baseline pass rates than middle schools, so combining the separated groups produces a negative overall trend even though each within-level trend is positive.
· Point 2: Identifies school level as a lurking or confounding variable associated with both average tutoring minutes and pass rate; aggregation masks the within-level relationships.
(d) 2 points
· Point 1: Rejects the causal claim because the data are observational and schools were not randomly assigned tutoring amounts; factors such as course difficulty, student age, prior achievement, or allocation of tutoring to higher-need schools could explain the association.
· Point 2: Uses the positive within-level slopes and correlations as evidence against the administrator's interpretation of the negative combined slope; the aggregated association does not show that additional tutoring lowers pass rates.
(e) 2 points
· Point 1: Calculates the all-school prediction as 93.156 − 0.271(70) = 74.186% and the high-school prediction as 51.800 + 0.300(70) = 72.800%.
· Point 2: Selects the high-school prediction as more appropriate because it is based on the relevant subgroup, 70 minutes lies within the observed high-school range, and the subgroup relationship avoids the distortion caused by combining school levels.
questions.modelResponse:
The scatterplot should reveal two distinct clusters. Within each cluster, pass rate rises as tutoring time rises. Because the high-school cluster is farther right and lower than the middle-school cluster, the combined cloud slopes downward. This reversal is an aggregation effect caused by school level, which is related to both variables.

The combined line predicts about 79.6% at 50 minutes, but no observed school is near 50 minutes and the two levels occupy different ranges. The negative combined slope is an association, not an effect of assigning more tutoring. The study is observational, and the positive subgroup slopes directly undermine a causal reading of the combined slope. For a 70-minute high school, the subgroup prediction of 72.8% is preferable to the combined prediction of about 74.2% because it uses the relevant within-level pattern. Even the subgroup line remains descriptive rather than causal.
